# Abstract

The reconstruction of who-infected-whom is an important component of infectious disease outbreak analysis, and numerous methods have been developed to infer transmission histories from epidemiological and genomic data.
However, exploring the resulting transmission networks remains challenging, particularly when considering uncertainty, associated metadata, and results from different inference methods.

Here, we present CONTAGION, an interactive framework for the visualization and exploratory analysis of inferred who-infected-whom networks.
CONTAGION provides a locally running, browser-based interface for interactively exploring transmission relationships, uncertainty, and associated metadata.
It supports output from several commonly used transmission-inference methods as well as general network formats, providing a consistent visualization environment across different approaches.
By separating visualization from the underlying inference method, CONTAGION provides a flexible and extensible framework for investigating, comparing, and communicating inferred transmission networks.

# Impact Statement

To better control and prevent infectious diseases it is important to understand the underlying transmission dynamics.
There are many different methods to reconstruct and model  these dynamics, however, at the end of many is the reconstruction of a likely who-infected-whom scenario.
Having an easy to use interactive dashboard to explore the results of an inference method with different parameter settings in combination with additional metadata for individuals can significantly improve the understanding of transmission pathways.

We present CONTAGION as a complementary layer of visualization among the ever growing collection of transmission inference methods and software.
It provides consistent visualization among methods, is easy to extend, and unifies the sharing, comparing, or interpreting of who-infected-whom networks.

# Introduction

Understanding and reconstructing transmission dynamics is an important component of infectious disease outbreak analysis. A wide range of computational methods have therefore been developed to reconstruct transmission histories from epidemiological, genomic, and contact-tracing data [@jombart2014outbreaker; @demaio2016scotti; @klinkenberg2017phybreak; @campbell2018outbreaker2]; for a systematic comparison of many of these approaches, see [@duault2022methods]. These methods differ substantially in the data they require, the processes they model, and the assumptions they make about pathogen evolution and transmission. For example, some approaches operate directly on pairwise genetic distances, whereas others infer transmission from a phylogenetic tree or jointly infer phylogenetic and transmission histories. Regardless of the methodological approach, these methods ultimately represent the inferred transmission history as a who-infected-whom network or transmission tree, providing a common object through which transmission histories can be inspected.

Widely used who-infected-whom inference methods such as outbreaker2  [@campbell2018outbreaker2], TransPhylo [@didelot2017transphylo], SCOTTI [@demaio2016scotti], BREATH  [@colijn2026breath], and PhyBreak [@klinkenberg2017phybreak] typically begin with information from pathogen sequences and the timing of infection or sampling, but differ in how they model transmission, pathogen evolution, unsampled infections, and uncertainty, resulting in outputs that are not visualized in the same way [@duault2022methods; @sobkowiak2023comparing]. Outbreaker2 which uses a Bayesian framework to combine pathogen sequence data, sampling times, a generation time distribution, and optionally contact tracing data to yield a posterior summary of infectors, number of intermediate transmission generations, infection times and model parameters, summarized in a transmission tree [@campbell2018outbreaker2]. TransPhylo on the other hand, takes a timed phylogenetic tree as input and uses a branching process to model transmission allowing for unsampled hosts within inferred transmission chains [@didelot2017transphylo]. This results in a posterior distribution of transmission trees including unsampled hosts. PhyBreak takes in sequences and sampling times and simultaneously samples the phylogenetic tree and transmission tree, resulting in a posterior that contains infectors, infection times, phylogenetic relationships and associated model parameters [@klinkenberg2017phybreak]. SCOTTI treats each host as a population in a structured coalescent and models transmission as migration between hosts [@demaio2016scotti]. This lets it account for multiple samples from the same host, within-host evolution and unsampled hosts and results in a posterior of host-transition histories. Finally, BREATH simultaneously infers phylogenetic and transmission trees while allowing unsampled individuals, within-host evolution, and flexible infection natural histories [@colijn2026breath].  While all of these methods aim to accomplish the same thing, differences in their summarized output, such as if unsampled hosts are included or not, mean that visualization of the who-infected-whom information resulting from these methods are not necessarily directly comparable or visualized in the same way [@firestone2019reconstructing; @sobkowiak2023comparing].

Some effort has been made to separate transmission network visualization from inference. TGV [@phelan2024TVG], for example, introduced a general JSON representation for transmission graphs, together with tools for converting and manipulating transmission inference outputs and an interactive browser based interface for exploring nodes, edges, and associated metadata. More broadly, interactive genomic epidemiology platforms such as Microreact [@argimon2016microreact], Nextstrain [@hadfield2018nextstrain], and HAIviz  [@permana2024haiviz] have demonstrated the utility of linking phylogenies with temporal, geographic, and epidemiological metadata rather than relying on static figures. HAIviz, for example, combines transmission networks with patient movement, timelines, phylogenetic trees, and hospital location data to support investigation of healthcare-associated outbreaks [@permana2024haiviz]. These tools demonstrate the value of interactive exploration, but generally target particular forms of genomic epidemiological data or particular outbreak settings rather than providing a general analysis layer for outputs from multiple who-infected-whom inference frameworks.

The lack of a common visualization and analysis layer presents challenges for both exploratory analysis and comparison of transmission inference methods [@firestone2019reconstructing; @sobkowiak2023comparing; @phelan2024TVG]. Researchers may need to use different tools or construct separate visualizations depending on the software used to generate a network. Moreover, visualizations are often presented as static images, requiring decisions about which transmission events, annotations, and other network properties should be displayed before the figure is generated. This can be particularly restrictive for probabilistic transmission reconstruction, where changing a probability threshold may reveal a different set of plausible transmission relationships, or where several alternative infectors may have substantial posterior support. Exploring alternative representations from the same analysis output can consequently require repeatedly modifying and regenerating figures and then comparing several separate images. Similar limitations of static representations have motivated interactive visualization tools in genomic epidemiology more broadly [@argimon2016microreact; @phelan2024TVG]. These issues become increasingly important when investigating large networks or when an inferred transmission history is associated with substantial uncertainty or extensive epidemiological metadata.

Here, we present CONTAGION, an interactive visualization application for exploring who-infected-whom networks produced by multiple transmission-inference software tools. CONTAGION provides a common visualization layer between transmission-inference methods and the subsequent exploration of their results up to the generation of publication ready figures. Outputs from different software packages can be translated into a common network representation and explored through a unified interface. The application provides interactive control over network visualization, including filtering transmission events, changing edge-support thresholds, modifying node and edge annotations and shapes, and rearranging the network's layout. Additional individual-level metadata can be incorporated into the visualization and used to explore the network and the inferred dynamics. By bringing these capabilities together in a single application, CONTAGION allows users to interactively investigate transmission networks without having to construct separate visualizations for each inference method or parameter threshold setting. At the time of writing, CONTAGION supports outputs from several transmission-inference approaches, including SCOTTI, outbreaker2, TransPhylo, and BREATH, as well as custom network representations (TODO might have to add more, thinking about phybreak for example, also want to support general dot files).

# Theory and Implementation

## Who-infected-whom networks

To understand transmission dynamics, studies infer transmission trees and aim to reconstruct who-infected-whom relationships, providing information that can help characterize outbreaks and target control and preventative measures.
These reconstructions can be represented as a directed graph, where nodes correspond to individuals and edges represent transmission events from an infector to the individual they infected.
Such networks can be used to investigate transmission routes, characterize heterogeneous infectiousness and likely super-spreading events, and identify important transmission contexts such as households or facilities.
At the population level, the network may also reveal clusters and larger structures within an outbreak.

For their reconstruction, different combinations of epidemiological and genomic information, including sampling dates, contact-tracing information, geographical information, and pathogen sequence data, are used.
Existing inference methods differ in how these sources of information are incorporated and in the assumptions made about the transmission process.
A recent review article of such methods groups them into three families: sequential phylogenetic, simultaneous phylogenetic, and non-phylogenetic approaches (TODO cite duault).

Inference typically involves uncertainty and therefore results in a multitude of possible transmission histories rather than a single definitive reconstruction.
These possible histories can be summarized as a transmission network that captures the uncertainty in the inferred relationships.
For example, outbreaker2 uses MCMC to sample transmission chains, while TransPhylo and BREATH can account for unsampled individuals in the reconstructed transmission tree.
The resulting transmission relationships should therefore be interpreted in the context of this uncertainty associated with the inference method.

Visualizing the inferred transmission networks alongside additional information allows a comparison between the inferred and known or independently established information.
This can be useful for assessing whether particular transmission relationships are compatible with known contact patterns, sampling dates, locations, or other outbreak information.
Individual samples are also commonly associated with metadata describing the individuals involved, such as age, sex, geographical location, household, or sampling date.
Such information provides additional context for interpreting the inferred transmission history and can reveal patterns that are not apparent from the network structure alone.

## Our proposed layer of visualization

While inference methods focus primarily on reconstructing complex transmission networks, researchers must subsequently explore and interpret the resulting networks.
This exploration is often performed using static visualizations or separate, method-specific workflows.

Static network visualization require many aspects of the network to be fixed in advance.
For example, an edge posterior-support threshold may determine which transmission relationships are displayed, while node colors, metadata attributes, and network layouts are fixed for a particular figure.
Exploring a different combination of settings such as different thresholds, comparing different metadata, or rearranging a densely connected network therefore requires generating a new image from the beginning.
These limitations become particularly relevant for large networks, where changing the layout, manually repositioning nodes, or changing edge threshold values may help reveal individual transmission relationships and larger network structures.

We present CONTAGION as an interactive visualization layer for transmission-inference methods.
It provides a common interface through which users can explore the inferred network, its uncertainty, and associated metadata without constructing separate visualizations for each analysis.
Inference-specific output formats are converted into a common representation, allowing the same visualization and exploration functionality to be applied across different inference approaches.

## Implementation details

Our application is implemented in Python using the Dash framework [@parmer2025dash] for the web interface and
Cytoscape.js [@franz2016cytoscapejs], through the dash-cytoscape component, for interactive graph visualization.
The application runs locally or can be deployed as a web service, allowing users to explore the networks
directly within a browser.

Internally, the software has a modular architecture separating data handling, visualization, and user interface logic.
Each upload parser converts the inferred transmission data into a standard graph representation of nodes and edges.
Metadata is added to the node data and this representation is then shared between visualization and analytical components.
Interactive components such as filtering, coloring, metadata inspection, and network statistics
(e.g. node degree distributions or metadata-specific graph connectivity) are implemented through Dash callback functions that re-actively update only the affected interface elements.

The application is open source (under a TODO license) and easily extendable to new input types, since each upload format has its own parser but all parsers use the same graph representation format.
All code and a tutorial website with associated data is available on github [https://github.com/Lars-B/interactive-wiw].
The application is also packaged, via a GitHub Actions build pipeline, into a single executable for each major platform, available for download from the repository releases [https://github.com/Lars-B/interactive-wiw/releases/latest].

## Application to a tuberculosis outbreak

To demonstrate how the interactive visualization can be used to explore inferred transmission histories,
we applied it to a tuberculosis outbreak data set analyzed with the BREATH package [@colijn2024breath].
Rather than attempting to establish a single definitive reconstruction of this particular outbreak, we use this example to illustrate how inferred transmission relationships, their associated uncertainty, and individual-level metadata can be explored and compared within a common visualization framework.

We focus on several representative questions that commonly arise when interpreting reconstructed transmission networks:
identifying likely sources of individual infections, examining cases for which no sampled source is strongly supported, tracing transmission involving individuals of particular interest, and exploring associations between epidemiological metadata and transmission patterns.

### Exploring different metadata

In addition to examining individual transmission relationships, the inferred networks can be explored in the context of associated epidemiological metadata.
Nodes can be colored according to variables such as sampling date, smear positivity, residence status, or reported alcohol and drug use, allowing potential patterns to be examined without constructing separate visualizations for each variable.
This makes it possible to visually assess, for example, whether particular characteristics are concentrated among individuals with multiple inferred downstream infections.
Such visual associations are intended primarily for exploratory analysis and should not, by themselves, be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships.

# Discussion

<!-- Contribution and why tool is good idea -->
Inference methods for the reconstruction of infectious disease outbreaks are increasingly becoming more diverse with many available software tools TODOcite.
Interactive visualization approaches provide an important complement to these computational methods for analyzing the inferred transmission reconstruction together with additional metadata.
While statistical and phylogenetic approaches can infer the transmission relationships, visual exploration remains valuable for understanding the resulting structures and communicate findings.
Our application CONTAGION bridges this gap by providing an input agnostic interface to examine and explore inferred who-infected-whom networks interactively.
A common interface for these different methods in a valuable way to analyses and investigate findings for users but also an important tool when sharing findings with others in a unified way.

<!-- Where does it fit in and who is this for -->
Our tool, CONTAGION, separates the visualization of a transmission network from the software tool used to infer the network.
This allows networks generated by different approaches to be inspected using the same visual conventions and interaction mechanisms,
making comparisons between results from different methods easier.
A further advantage of CONTAGION is its accessibility to users without programming or terminal experience.
The browser-based interface allows transmission networks to be explored without writing code,
while the configurable interface allows users to adapt the visualization to different datasets and use cases.

<!-- strengths of our app approach -->
Existing transmission-reconstruction software may provide visualization functionality, while general-purpose network visualization tools can also be used to display transmission networks.
CONTAGION combines the strength of both in focusing specifically on inferred who-infected-whom networks and in providing a common interface across multiple transmission reconstruction methods.
An additional advantage of a shared visualization framework is that it can make aspects of a reconstruction that are implicit in the underlying model more accessible to users.
In particular, CONTAGION provides a means of investigating indirect transmission relationships represented in the transmission trees produced by transphylo and BREATH.
These relationships might not be immediately apparent when examining the underlying output alone.
Using the same visualization framework also promotes consistency in how transmission reconstructions are presented,
reducing ambiguous or unclear differences in visual representation that arise solely from the different software used to generate it.

<!-- Limitations of our app -->
Our browser based architecture introduces a practical limitation.
Specifically for phylogenetic tree inference the output files are often large and require substantial time to upload and parse.
Browser based file handling may limit the size of datasets that can be conveniently explored.
These limitations represent a trade-off for the accessibility and ease of use provided by a browser-based application.
The need to support method-specific output formats also illustrates the potential value of standardized transmission-network representations.
Such a common representation could facilitate interoperability between inference methods, visualization tools, and downstream analysis.

<!--Future directions and wrap up -->
A natural extension of this application would be to include quantitative summaries and comparison measures of networks directly into the application.
For example, network-level statistics and metric used to compare transmission reconstructions could allow users not only to visually inspect networks,
but also to assess similarities and differences between reconstructions.
CONTAGION complements rather than competes with inference methods by providing a
common interface through which their outputs can be explored, interpreted, compared, and communicated.
